project.name: app/greeter.iyi
project.text:
# The dependency. Its exported surface is the whole of what a consumer, or an
# agent editing one, is allowed to know: two functions with their types
# written down, and a trait. `greeting` has no `pub`, so it is this module's
# own business and appears in no consumer's grounding (SPEC.md R-1, IV.2).
module app/greeter

pub trait Greet
  abstract def greet : String
end

# The exported surface carries its doc comment, so the grounding pack an agent
# reads says what the function is for and not only what it takes.
pub def polite(name : String) : String
  "#{greeting}, #{name}."
end

pub def shout(name : String) : String
  "#{greeting.upcase}, #{name.upcase}!"
end

def greeting : String
  "Hello"
end

project.name: app.iyi
project.text:
# The file being edited, in the state an agent meets it: one call misspelled.
# The compiler knows the name it meant, so `iyi check -f json` carries a
# `suggested_edit` with the exact replacement span and `iyi fix` applies it.
module app

import app/greeter
using app/greeter

pub def main : Int32
  puts polit("Türkiye")
  0
end

project.name: app_test.iyi
project.text:
# A test is a plain program that exits non-zero when it fails; the prelude's
# `assert` is that in one word. No framework, so nothing here has to be
# learned before it can be read.
module app/app_test

import app/greeter
using app/greeter

assert polite("iyi") == "Hello, iyi.", "polite greets"
assert shout("iyi") == "HELLO, IYI!", "shout shouts"

project.name: other.iyi
project.text:
# Imported by nothing. It is here so `iyi test --affected` has a change it can
# prove no test reaches, which is the half of test selection that is easy to
# claim and hard to show.
module app/other

pub def unrelated : Int32
  0
end

frames.title: Read the interface, not the repository
frames.note: Every import's exported surface as data: signatures, doc comments and the interface hash they are keyed by, with no body anywhere in it. Read out of source, without compiling the file being edited, so it is available while the program is still wrong.

frames.title: The verdict as data
frames.note: `check` is a build with no codegen and its name said plainly. Under `-f json` each error is a record: the file, the line, the column, the span's size, the message, and a `suggested_edit` naming the exact replacement when the compiler knows one.

frames.title: Apply the compiler's own edit
frames.note: `fix` applies the suggested edits and recompiles after each one, until the file is clean or an error carries no edit. The agent spends no round on a repair the compiler already knows how to make.

frames.title: Green, and silent about it
frames.note: The verdict is the exit code, so a clean program prints nothing. There is no output for a harness to parse for the word success.

frames.title: Re-run what the change reaches
frames.note: A test is affected exactly when the changed file is in its transitive import closure. The closure is parsed, never compiled, because R-1 makes the import list syntax.

frames.title: And skip what it does not
frames.note: The same question about a module nothing imports. The selection is exact, so the skip is a fact rather than an optimisation that might be wrong.
frames.stdout: 0 to run, 1 skipped: no test's imports reach the change

frames.title: The run as data
frames.note: `--json` for a harness that has to read the result rather than a person who reads it.

frames.title: A body moved, so nobody rebuilds
frames.note: One module's greeting changed and its declarations did not. `mod diff` reads the two artifacts and answers whether the change reaches anyone, which is the question the whole rule exists to make answerable.

Consumers do not have to be rebuilt: what they compile against is the same.

frames.title: A declaration moved, so they do
frames.note: The same file again, with one exported signature written differently. The artifact names what went and what arrived, so a consumer's rebuild is a consequence rather than a guess.
